scenario: A software engineering manager compares bug introduction rates for two development teams (A and B) across junior and senior engineers. Team B reports a higher overall bug rate, so the manager prepares to retrain Team B. A senior engineer challenges the conclusion.

data.description: Bug rates (bugs introduced per 100 commits) by seniority level and team. Lower is better.

question: Team B's overall bug rate (16.6%) is far higher than Team A's (6.5%). The manager plans to retrain Team B. (a) Which team has a lower bug rate among junior engineers? (b) Which team has a lower bug rate among senior engineers? (c) If both teams had equal numbers of junior and senior engineers (50/50), which team would have the lower corrected bug rate? Compute both corrected rates.

ground_truth.explanation: Team B has a lower bug rate at both experience levels. The manager's conclusion is wrong. Team B's higher aggregate rate is caused by composition: Team B is 90% senior engineers (who introduce more bugs regardless of team) while Team A is 90% junior engineers. Team B is actually the better team.

naive_answer: Team A, because its overall bug rate of 6.5% is far lower than Team B's 16.6%.
naive_trap: Team A is staffed overwhelmingly with junior engineers who commit low-risk changes. Team B is staffed overwhelmingly with senior engineers who work on complex, higher-risk code. Comparing aggregate bug rates ignores experience-level composition entirely.
